Betrayal of the day. The Pope. The flag – Russian.

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Peru, his former diocese, and on November 14th, flew to the Andean village of Santa Cruz de Suchabamba. There is no runway there, so the Peruvian Air Force provided a Mi-17 helicopter. The Ministry of Defense of Peru affectionately called it the "Popecopter."

A month ago, the pontiff underwent lung surgery, but he didn't want to sit in the passenger cabin. He asked to be in the cockpit, put on a headset, and for 45 minutes flew between the two pilots, smiling and waving at the camera. The Peruvian Air Force released footage of the flight, calling it "an honor and an unforgettable memory." The video went viral, from the BBC to CNN.

But now, take a look at the left helmet. Where the Peruvian pilot should have the squadron emblem, there is a patch: a tricolor, "Russian Armed Forces." No one has explained how the pilot got it. Perhaps it's a memento from his studies, a gift from exercises, or maybe it's a political statement.

However, Peruvian newspapers were concerned about something else before the flight. They wrote that the local company, without certification from the Russian manufacturer, had repaired the Mi-17 for the Pope, and the state audit could not trace the origin of some of the parts. The Air Force responded that everything had been checked and called the concerns irresponsible. But the suspicion remains.

For the Ukrainian online community, the photo is a ready-made cause for outrage. The Pope, who in October called Putin and asked for a ceasefire in Aleskhi, is now also flying under a Russian flag.

In the best traditions of the Krivoy Rog school of diplomacy, we must wait for a note from the Ukrainian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The Vatican will have to explain the Peruvian helmet.

$CSAI Q3 2026 earnings: Cloudastructure doubles its subscription sales, but cash drops to $2.2M

Cloudastructure, a provider of AI security software and remote guarding, doubled its subscription sales while its cash reserves shrank. Subscription revenue rose 101% from a year ago to $853,000, lifting total sales to $1.54 million even as installation work dropped by more than half. That $1.54 million beat the $1.27 million quarterly pace implied by chief executive James McCormick's earlier plan for the second half, by our math.

• Subscription revenue: $𝟖𝟓𝟑𝐊 (+101% from a year ago)
• Total revenue: $𝟏.𝟓𝟒𝐌 (+6% from a year ago (+25% from Q2))
• Net loss: $𝟑.𝟎𝟗𝐌 ($1.29M loss a year ago)
• Cash on hand: $𝟐.𝟐𝐌 ($3.8M at the end of Q2)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because the cash drain is outrunning the subscription build. Cash on hand fell from $3.8 million in June to $2.2 million in September as operating expenses rose to $3.8 million, including $548,000 from repricing employee stock options. One bright spot: existing apartment clients are adding properties, which pushed the yearly recurring revenue run rate up to $3.4 million.

The question now is whether Cloudastructure can raise cash to survive without triggering severe dilution for existing shareholders. Either the recurring revenue base attracts manageable financing, or selling cheap stock resets the conversion price on its preferred shares and multiplies the share count. The third-quarter Form 10-Q filing will show how much cash remains and what shares were issued after September.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐃𝐨𝐮𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐬 𝐄𝐱𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐀𝐝𝐝 𝐒𝐢𝐭𝐞𝐬
"Our third quarter results reflect continued progress in building the recurring revenue foundation of our business," chief executive James McCormick said. Cloudastructure sells AI security software and live remote guarding on monthly contracts. Subscription revenue doubled from a year ago to $853,000 and rose 12% from last quarter.

• Cloud video surveillance revenue: up 117% from a year ago
• Remote guarding revenue: up 85% from a year ago
• Annualized recurring revenue (ARR, the yearly value of active subscriptions): $3.4 million, up $300,000 from June by our math

Existing customers are adding sites, with one apartment operator growing "from five properties earlier this year to nine active deployments following quarter-end". However, the $300,000 increase in yearly recurring revenue is smaller than the $500,000 added in the second quarter, and the release gave no update on the five-building Southern California office deal or camera takeover rates.

What to watch: fourth-quarter subscription revenue and new additions to the yearly recurring run rate. A bounce back to $500,000 in quarterly additions would show the new sales leadership is speeding up contract wins.

🟢 𝐑𝐞𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐢𝐱 𝐊𝐞𝐞𝐩𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝟓𝟎%
Cloudastructure makes a higher profit margin on monthly monitoring software than on physical camera installation. Because subscriptions rose from 29% of total sales a year ago to 55% this quarter, gross profit rose 9% to $785,000 and gross margin reached 51%, up 1.4 percentage points from a year ago and 2 points from the second quarter.

What to watch: the breakdown of cost of goods sold by service line in the upcoming quarterly filing. In the second quarter, installation labor costs exceeded installation sales, so the filing will show whether installation work now covers its own labor.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐩𝐬 𝐭𝐨 $𝟐.𝟐 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐖𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧
McCormick said the security company is spending more on sales, marketing and operations "to support customer acquisition, deployments and the expansion of remote guarding" while aiming for efficiency as it grows. In practice, costs are rising much faster than revenue, and cash on hand fell by $1.6 million during the quarter to $2.2 million.

• Total operating expenses: $3.8 million, up 61 percentage points of revenue from a year ago by our math
• General and administrative overhead: $1.4 million, up 22 percentage points of revenue on legal and professional fees
• Sales, marketing, research and operations: $2.4 million, up 39 percentage points of revenue by our math

Even after stripping out non-cash items like stock pay, the quarterly loss excluding one-offs widened by 76% from a year ago to $2.1 million. That spending pace cuts against management's claim of scaling toward efficiency, because $785,000 in gross profit covers just one-fifth of operating overhead. At a $1.6 million quarterly cash drain, $2.2 million leaves little more than one quarter of cash.

What to watch: cash raised from stock sales or credit lines in the third-quarter filing and after September 30. Without new funding, cash on hand would run critically low before the end of the first quarter of 2027.

🔴 𝐒𝐡𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐈𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐖𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐇𝐨𝐥𝐝𝐬 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐭𝐨 𝟔%
While monthly subscriptions doubled, installation and other revenue dropped 60% from a year ago to $274,000, down from $679,000 in the third quarter of 2025. That drop pulled total revenue growth down to 6% from a year ago, continuing a sharp slowdown from 78% growth in the first quarter and 13% in the second.

Total sales did bounce back 25% from the second quarter to $1.54 million as hardware sales rose 77% to $412,000. That clears the $1.27 million quarterly pace needed to beat first-half sales, as management planned, but fourth-quarter total sales still face a tough comparison against roughly $1.8 million a year ago.

What to watch: fourth-quarter hardware and installation revenue. If installation sales stay near $274,000, total fourth-quarter revenue will shrink compared with a year ago even if subscriptions keep growing.

🔴 𝐎𝐩𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐬 $𝟓𝟒𝟖,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐢𝐧 𝐍𝐨𝐧-𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬
Third-quarter operating expenses included $548,000 of non-cash stock compensation "related to the repricing of stock options on August 27, 2026". Lowering the exercise price on employee options after the shares fell added a charge equal to 36% of quarterly revenue by our math, pushing total stock-based pay to $878,000, or 57% of revenue.

What to watch: the stock compensation footnote in the third-quarter filing. It will disclose whether the $548,000 charge settled the entire option repricing or leaves more expense to be recognized over future quarters.

🔴🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
The earnings release did not include a balance sheet, a cash flow statement, or share counts, leaving four survival and dilution risks unreadable until the quarterly filing arrives.

• Financing cash flows and Equity Line expiry: the release does not state whether Cloudastructure tapped its at-the-market stock facility or replaced its $50 million equity line before its November 2026 expiration.
• Preferred stock dilution reset and debt conversions: the quarterly filing will show how many common shares were issued to pay monthly installments on the $1.3 million promissory note and whether any stock sales triggered a lower conversion price on the Series 2 preferred shares.
• Nasdaq market-value listing rule: without a current share count, readers cannot check the company's market value of listed securities against minimum exchange thresholds.
• Filing timeliness: after two straight late quarterly filings, the release gave no filing date for the third-quarter Form 10-Q.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐂𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐭𝐞𝐬 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫-𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐋𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐮𝐩
After the quarter ended, the Palo Alto group launched a configurable powered enclosure on October 20, 2026. The unit completes a four-product deployable surveillance lineup designed to bring AI video monitoring to sites with limited electrical power and internet connectivity. The company has not yet reported sales figures for the enclosure.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐇𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟒𝟏𝟐 𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐚𝐧𝐝  ⇄ reversing
Hardware revenue — sales of Cloud Video Recorders and camera gear — rose 18.7% from a year ago and rebounded 76.8% from $233 thousand in the second quarter. In the second quarter, hardware sales had dropped by nearly half as more customers connected existing cameras instead of buying new equipment.

𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐠𝐨𝐨𝐝𝐬 𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐝 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟕𝟓𝟒 𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐬𝐚𝐧𝐝  ⇒ stable

Adjusted EBITDA — operating loss excluding stock-based pay, depreciation, taxes and non-cash financing items — widened 76.2% from a $1.20 million loss a year ago. Compared with the first quarter's $2.14 million loss, the quarterly cash operating deficit held roughly steady as higher gross profit offset rising overhead.

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

Cash dropped by $1.6 million in the third quarter to $2.2 million, and the $50 million equity line was set to expire around November 2026. Investors need to know what funding source remains available and whether using it resets the Series 2 preferred conversion price.

By our math, the annualized recurring revenue run rate rose by $300,000 in the third quarter, down from $500,000 in the second quarter and $600,000 in the first. Management did not disclose how much growth came from new customers versus existing property expansions.

𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐒𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐂𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐚 𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐨 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞?

On January 19, 2026, a six-foot-diameter section of the Potomac Interceptor collapsed near Washington, D.C. Maryland’s Department of the Environment estimates that 243 million gallons of untreated wastewater were released into the Potomac River. 
A single failure in a buried pipe became a regional environmental emergency.
Originally constructed in the 1960s, the interceptor carries up to 60 million gallons of wastewater daily. Crews built an emergency bypass, operated pumps and repaired the damaged section. Normal flow returned on March 14, nearly two months after the collapse. Drinking-water supplies were unaffected, but the incident required extensive emergency work and environmental monitoring. 
For cities around the world, the event raises an uncomfortable question: how well do we understand the condition of the essential infrastructure beneath our feet?
For SewerVUE Technologies, a NameSilo Technologies ($URL.C) subsidiary, that question sits at the centre of a substantial business opportunity.
A wake-up call for infrastructure owners
Wastewater keeps arriving even when the pipe carrying it fails. Containing the flow, accessing the damage and completing repairs can become a major engineering undertaking.
Importantly, the Potomac Interceptor was not an uninspected asset. In its March assessment, DC Water said four internal inspections over seven years had identified exposed aggregate and surface reinforcement but had not indicated imminent structural failure. The utility also commissioned an independent review of its assessments and methodology. 
That history highlights the difficulty of translating inspection findings into an understanding of structural risk. It does not establish that SewerVUE could have predicted or prevented this particular collapse. It does strengthen the case for comprehensive condition data and careful engineering interpretation.
For utilities managing extensive buried networks, the challenge is deciding which assets require attention before an emergency forces the decision.
Looking beyond the camera
Cameras provide valuable information about a pipe’s visible interior. But images alone cannot reliably establish how much material remains within the wall or whether a cavity is developing outside it.
SewerVUE’s distinguishing technology is its patented pipe-penetrating radar, or PPR. Applied from inside suitable pipes, it can measure remaining wall thickness and reinforcement cover, and identify indications of delamination and external voids. These findings help engineers investigate conditions that conventional visual inspection cannot resolve on its own.
 
Complementary sensors add further information. LiDAR measures geometry above the waterline; profiling sonar examines submerged geometry and sediment; CCTV supplies visual context. The appropriate combination depends on the asset and operating conditions. 
The commercial value comes from what utilities can do with those measurements: refine rehabilitation plans, investigate hidden deterioration and direct spending toward the assets that need it most.
A global problem with a long runway
The potential scale is substantial. The American Society of Civil Engineers’ 2025 report card describes approximately 1.87 million miles of U.S. wastewater conveyance pipes, roughly three million kilometres, and gives wastewater infrastructure a D+.  infrastructurereportcard.org
Across established urban networks worldwide, age creates a reason to investigate. It does not automatically mean a pipe requires replacement. Materials, operating conditions and the surrounding environment influence how individual assets deteriorate.
That distinction matters. Replacing sound infrastructure prematurely consumes scarce capital. Leaving seriously deteriorated assets in service can expose communities to costly failures.
Better inspection can help engineers make more informed choices between monitoring, localized repair, rehabilitation and replacement.
The financial backdrop reinforces the need for careful allocation. The EPA’s 2022 Clean Watersheds Needs Survey identified US$630.1 billion in clean-water infrastructure needs over 20 years, expressed in January 2022 dollars. This includes wastewater, stormwater and other eligible projects; it measures the broader infrastructure challenge rather than the inspection market.  www.epa.gov
Turning need into business
For SewerVUE, the opportunity is to win a share of spending on condition assessments, equipment, rentals and related services for suitable assets.
Critical sewer trunks and difficult-to-access mains offer a compelling starting point because the consequences of failure can be significant. SewerVUE’s tracked robots and floating platforms provide different deployment options, including inspection of flowing mains using its MPIS Float in suitable conditions. 
Successful projects could lead to broader inspections within a network, relationships with engineering consultants and regional partners, and repeat assessments as assets age.
Execution will determine the business outcome. Investors should watch for repeat customers, wider adoption, profitable delivery and conversion of technical capability into cash flow.
The Potomac collapse shows how quickly a buried asset can become a public emergency. SewerVUE’s opportunity is to help utilities understand their critical pipes more thoroughly and make better decisions before the next failure brings another sewer into the headlines.

Daily spend limit per member. In Teams you can cap what each person or agent spends per day, with one figure for everyone or a custom one per person. More than a hundred years ago the Soviet director Lev Kuleshov cut the same close-up of the film star Ivan Mosjoukine's blank face next to three other shots: a bowl of soup, a girl in a coffin, a woman on a divan. Audiences swore the actor played hunger, grief and desire. The face never changed. The cut did the acting.
That is the Kuleshov effect, and in November 2026 it is the whole game in AI video.
 
Shots got cheap:
Nov 5. Google released Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: clips up to 15 seconds for $0.07 a second, 30% cheaper than before, with editing by conversation
Sep 30. HeyGen's own video model went out through an API at $0.01 a second as a launch price, with sound generated in the same call
Nov 13. Krea opened a beta of Krea Bots, a crew of agents (director, storyboard, edit, motion, sound) that runs a whole creative project
HyperFrames, HeyGen's open-source tool that turns HTML into MP4, passed 84K stars on GitHub, because coding agents can now build animation the same way they build a web page
Embed here: @GoogleAIStudio "Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash: Fast and cost-effective with longer clips" (Nov 5)
Embed here: @krea_ai "introducing Krea Bots, your new creative crew" (Nov 13)
So anyone can now get a beautiful 8-second shot. Most AI videos still look like a slot machine: random shots in a row, a different face in every clip, music that ignores the cut.
This roadmap is about the part that is still yours: the format, the script, the shot list, consistency between shots, and the edit. Every tool in it works from Europe and from the US with a normal account and a card. Every step has the setup, the real price per second and the place where it breaks.
By the end you will have one repeatable pipeline that turns an idea into a 30-second ad, a 60-second explainer or a short for X, and you will know what each finished second cost.
 
01. Pick one format and one length before you open any tool
The slot-machine problem starts here. People open a video model, type an idea and hope. Decide the box first, because the box decides everything after it.
Three formats cover most of what people actually post and sell:
Product ad, 15 to 30 seconds, vertical 9:16 or square. One product, one problem, one moment where it works.
Explainer, 45 to 90 seconds, horizontal 16:9. One idea, shown in steps, with a voice over.
Short for X, 20 to 40 seconds, square or 16:9. One surprising thing, shown in the first 2 seconds.
Then do the arithmetic. Video models make clips of a few seconds: Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash goes from 3 to 15 seconds, HeyGen Video from 5 to 15. A 30-second ad cut at a normal pace is 10 to 15 shots, not one long generation.
Write it down as one line and keep it on top of every file:
 
If you can't fill ONE MESSAGE in under ten words, no model will fix it later.
02. Script and shot list before any generation
Generation is the expensive part, so the thinking happens in text, where a rewrite costs nothing. Give your format line to Claude or ChatGPT with this prompt:
 
The GEN / CODE / REAL column is the part that saves money. Text, interfaces, charts and diagrams are where video models fail most often (HeyGen itself lists long on-screen text as a known weakness of its model), and they are exactly what code does perfectly. Step 05 covers them.
Read the shot list out loud with a timer. If it doesn't fit, cut shots now, not after you paid for them.
 
03. Lock the look with three reference sheets
The fastest way to spot an AI video is a face or a product that changes between cuts. You fix that before generating a single clip, with three images you reuse in every shot:
A character sheet: the same person from the front, the side and three-quarters, neutral light, plain background
A product sheet: the product from 3 angles, true colours, logo readable
A style frame: one finished-looking still that sets the light, lens, colour grade and mood
Make them with any image model you already pay for. The prompt shape that keeps sheets usable:
 
Then feed the sheets to the video model instead of describing the person again. Both main video tools in this roadmap take references. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash accepts character, product and style images, plus motion clips up to 3 seconds and audio cues. HeyGen Video has a reference mode that takes up to 12 items in one call: 9 images, 3 videos and 3 audio clips.
One trap for Europe and the US. MiniMax's new open-weight image model H3-Image (released Nov 10) makes 16-megapixel images from up to 16 references, and the weights are free to download. Its licence grants rights only outside the EU, the UK, the US and South Korea, and that covers the images it produces too. If your clients are in those regions, the free weights are not free for you. Check the licence before you build a pipeline on any open model.
 
04. Generated shots: one action per clip, three takes, keep the best
Now the GEN rows of your shot list go to a video model. Two that matter this month:
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash (Google, Nov 5). $0.07 a second at 720p, 30% cheaper than the previous version, clips from 3 to 15 seconds. You can edit the same clip by conversation: swap the product or background, change the light or weather, switch the aspect ratio. It has multi-speaker lip-sync and every clip carries an invisible SynthID watermark. Developers get it through the Gemini API and Google AI Studio, and Google's list of Gemini API regions includes the EU, the UK and Ukraine. Google Vids also gives 15-second clips with a Google account or Workspace plan at no extra cost.
HeyGen Video (HeyGen, Sep 30). Made from text, an image or a set of references, with dialogue, ambience and effects generated in the same call. 5 to 15 seconds, 480p or 768p at 24 fps, from 21:9 to 9:16. The launch price was $0.01 a second through October, and the later standard rate isn't clearly published, so check your dashboard before a big batch. HeyGen lists its own weak spots: long on-screen text, soft organic motion and close hand work.
The shot prompt that works on both:
 
Three rules that save most of your takes:
One action per shot. "She opens the box" works. "She opens the box, smiles, turns to the window and waves" is four shots.
Write the change. A shot where nothing changes reads as a still with noise.
Draft cheap, finish once. Generate 3 takes per shot at draft quality, pick one, and only then upscale or re-render the winner.
The arithmetic for a 30-second ad: 12 shots of 4 seconds with 3 takes each is 144 generated seconds. At $0.07 a second on Omni that is about $10 for every take you will ever need, before the edit.
 
05. Code-built shots: let a coding agent animate what models get wrong
The CODE rows of your shot list are titles, prices, app screens, charts, diagrams and logos. A video model guesses letters. Code draws them exactly, renders the same way every time and costs nothing per second.
This is also where the most-watched AI animations on X come from. Fable 5.2 and Claude Code posts that went viral this autumn, like a "PC BUILD KIT" unboxing (103K views) or a wind-up cowboy toy (19.6K views), are animations written as code, not generated clips.
The tool that made this easy is HyperFrames, HeyGen's open-source framework: "Write HTML. Render video. Built for agents." It has about 84.7K stars on GitHub, runs under Apache 2.0 with no per-render fees, and needs only Node.js 22+ and FFmpeg. It renders each frame in headless Chrome and encodes with FFmpeg, so the same input always gives the same video.
Setup in Claude Code:
 
For Codex, Cursor and other agents: npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes. Without an agent:
 
Then describe the shot to your agent like a motion designer would:
 
HeyGen also shipped a video-specific agent inside HyperFrames Studio on November 14 and says it needs 30% less cost and 35% fewer model turns than Claude Code on the same video jobs. That is their own benchmark, so test both on your shot.
Where it breaks: code animation looks like motion graphics, not like film. Use it for the shots that carry information, and keep people, places and products in the GEN rows.
06. Sound first: voice, then music, then lip-sync
Most AI videos add sound at the end and it shows: cuts land between words, music swells on nothing. Flip the order. Sound is the clock the edit runs on.
Voice-over first. Record the script yourself or generate it with a text-to-speech model, then lock the timing. Every cut in step 08 will snap to this file. Fish Audio, for example, offers more than 2 million voices plus your own clone in one library.
Music second, cut to the voice. Leave a small gap in the music under the most important line, and land the biggest beat on the payoff shot.
Lip-sync last, only on shots where a face talks to camera. Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash has multi-speaker lip-sync, and HeyGen Video generates dialogue, ambience and effects together with the picture.
A prompt for a voice-over that sounds like a person:
 
Two rules that apply on both sides of the Atlantic:
Only clone a voice you own or have written permission to use. A cloned voice of a real person without consent is the fastest way to get a video taken down, and an account limited.
Use music you have a licence for. A model that generates music is fine only if its terms give you commercial rights to the output. Read that line before you put the track in a client ad.
 
07. Presenter videos: your digital twin for the talking parts
Some formats need a face talking to camera: a course lesson, a weekly update, a product demo in five languages. Filming each one is the slowest part of a video studio.
HeyGen released Avatar V on November 3. It renders talking-avatar video from a script or an audio track, using either a photo avatar or a digital twin. HeyGen says about 15 seconds of reference video is enough to start a twin, and output goes up to 1080p. One API reseller lists it at $0.12 per second, so a 60-second update is about $7, but check the price in your own HeyGen account.
How to make it look like you and not like a wax figure:
Record the reference in the light and framing you will actually use, looking into the lens, with natural pauses
Feed it the voice-over from step 06, not raw text, so the timing and stress are already right
Keep avatar shots short (4 to 8 seconds) and cut away to GEN and CODE shots, the way a TV presenter cuts to footage
The workflow that pays off fastest is translation. Record one master version, then render the same video with a voice-over in German, Polish, Spanish or Ukrainian. One shoot becomes five markets.
The rule for both regions is the same: only build a twin of yourself, or of someone who signed off on it in writing. In the EU there is also a legal line. Since 2 August 2026, the AI Act's transparency article requires anyone who publishes a deepfake, meaning realistic content that falsely appears authentic, to disclose that it is AI-generated. A short "AI presenter" label on screen or in the caption covers it and costs nothing.
08. The edit: where Kuleshov earns his money
You now have a voice-over, a music bed and a folder of shots: GEN clips, CODE renders, REAL recordings. The edit turns them into one idea. Two ways to do it with an agent.
The DIY route, free, works anywhere. Put everything in one folder with numbered files (shot01_gen.mp4, shot04_code.mp4, vo.wav, music.mp3) and give your coding agent this brief:
 
If you already use HyperFrames from step 05, it can do the same job: the whole edit becomes one HTML timeline with your clips as media, rendered to MP4.
The crew route, beta. Krea Bots are a team of agents in one chat. North is the creative director and pulls in specialists: Lumen for images, Doodle for storyboards, Snip for video edits, Glide for motion, Bloop for sound, Voxel for 3D, Serif for brand checks. They pick from more than 150 hosted image, video and audio models and do their editing on a private computer with Python, FFmpeg and ImageMagick. Access is a waitlist, beta teams get $1,000 in credits, and there is no public price yet.
Whatever does the cutting, you do the viewing. Watch the edit three times: once with sound off (does the picture alone tell the story?), once with eyes closed (does the voice alone?), and once at full speed on your phone, the way people will see it on X.
09. Know your cost per finished second, and who owns it
Price per generated second is the number on the launch post. The number that runs a studio is cost per finished second: everything you paid, divided by the seconds that end up in the final cut.
The math for the 30-second ad from this roadmap, at the prices above:
 
That is about $6.24 for the picture, or roughly 21 cents per finished second before sound. The takes you threw away are inside that number, which is the point: if your cost per finished second keeps rising, the shot list is the problem, not the model.
Three checks before anything goes to a client, from Europe or the US:
Licence of every model. Open weights are not always open to you: MiniMax H3-Image's licence excludes the EU, the UK, the US and South Korea, outputs included.
Labels. Gemini Omni clips carry an invisible SynthID watermark. In the EU, realistic content that could pass as real (a deepfake) must be disclosed as AI-generated since 2 August 2026. An "AI-generated" line in the caption is the cheap, safe default everywhere.
People and brands. No real person's face or voice without written consent, no other company's logo or product in your shots.
 
10. Examples of use
The pipeline is the same every time: format line, shot list, reference sheets, GEN and CODE shots, sound, edit. Five jobs it already handles:
A 30-second ad for a small online shop
One product, 12 shots, about $6 of generation, as in step 09.
How to repeat it: photograph the product on a plain background for the product sheet, write the format line with ONE MESSAGE in under ten words, and make the first 2 seconds the moment the product works.
A 60-second explainer built mostly from code
For ideas, numbers and processes, CODE shots carry the explanation and a few GEN shots add life.
Embed here: @HyperFrames_ "Our harness beats Claude Code: here's how" (Nov 14)
How to repeat it: ask for a shot list where at least 70% of shots are CODE, then build them all in one HyperFrames project so fonts and colours stay identical across the whole video.
One presenter, five languages
One recorded reference, one master script, five voice-overs, five renders of the same Avatar V video.
How to repeat it: translate the script with a prompt that keeps the length within 10% of the original, so the cuts still land, and label each version as an AI presenter.
Ten versions of one ad for testing
Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash edits a clip by conversation: the same shot with another background, other weather, other light or another aspect ratio.
How to repeat it: keep everything else in the edit fixed and change only the opening shot, so you learn which first 2 seconds hold attention.
A whole launch with a creative crew
Embed here: @krea_ai "introducing Krea Bots, your new creative crew" (Nov 13). Krea says all its own recent creative work was produced with these bots.
How to repeat it: join the beta waitlist, give North the format line and reference sheets from this roadmap as the brief, and keep the final edit review for yourself.
The shift
A year ago the hard part of AI video was getting one good shot. Now one good shot costs a few cents, and everyone has it.
What still separates a video people watch to the end from one they scroll past is what Kuleshov showed with a single face: the order of the shots, the length of each one, and the sound they sit on.
Start with one 30-second format, run the full pipeline once, and write down your cost per finished second. The second video goes faster, because the reference sheets and the shot list template are already done.

A wingtip met a nose on a Miami taxiway — and two federal investigations are now open.

- On Saturday night, Nov 14, a taxiing Copa Airlines Boeing 737-800's left wingtip struck the nose of a taxiing UPS Boeing 767-300 freighter at Miami International Airport.
- Air traffic controllers had instructed the UPS crew to give way to the arriving Copa aircraft before the collision (FAA).
- Copa Flight CM427 carried 166 passengers and six crew; two people were treated for minor injuries. The NTSB described the damage to the UPS aircraft as "substantial."
- The NTSB expects a preliminary report within 30 days, and the FAA is also investigating.

The full post below traces each of those points to its source — and the gallery report goes further, laying out the damage in detail, both investigations, the airline and airport responses, and what the safety literature says about how taxiway collisions happen.

Full report (TrustInsight gallery):
https://t.co/lUt6v3uQdW

—

1. THE COLLISION AT A GLANCE

A ground collision occurred at Miami International Airport on the night of Saturday 14 November 2026, when the left wingtip of a taxiing Copa Airlines Boeing 737-800 struck the nose of a taxiing UPS Boeing 767-300 freighter at the intersection of two taxiways.

The airport put the time at about 9:15 p.m. local; the FAA put it at around 9 p.m.

According to the FAA, air traffic controllers instructed the UPS crew to give way to the arriving Copa aircraft before the collision.

Sources: Fox News (https://t.co/hTzQUSvYHs); FAA statements (https://t.co/w4tzcWfinl); FLYING Magazine (https://t.co/yhi9snXPyh)

2. AIRCRAFT, FLIGHTS, DAMAGE AND INJURIES

The UPS aircraft was a Boeing 767-300 freighter operating as UPS Flight 358 (5X358), preparing to depart Miami for Bogotá, Colombia.

The Copa aircraft was Flight CM427, inbound from Panama City and taxiing to its gate, with 166 passengers and six crew aboard. Two people aboard were treated for minor injuries, described on Nov 16 as two passengers evaluated for minor injuries.

The NTSB said the Copa 737's wing struck the nose of the UPS 767 and described the damage to the UPS aircraft as "substantial." Photographs showed a horizontal gash on one side of the nose and a larger hole in the middle, and one account citing the NTSB described the forward fuselage as sliced open. FLYING Magazine reported on Nov 16 that both aircraft sustained substantial damage.

UPS said its crew was safe.

Sources: ABC News (https://t.co/H6RULk0SMA); PBS News (https://t.co/h85CQYbk6M); FLYING Magazine (link above)

3. INVESTIGATIONS AND RESPONSES

The FAA's statement said controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, that the collision occurred around 9 p.m. local time, and that the FAA is investigating.

The NTSB said on Nov 15 that it had opened an investigation and expected to release a preliminary report within 30 days.

UPS said it was aware of an incident involving one of its aircraft on the ground in Miami, that its crew was safe, and that it would work with authorities to determine what happened.

Miami International Airport said flights were being directed to other taxiways so there was no impact on airport operations. Airport communications director Greg Chin confirmed the collision occurred at about 9:15 p.m. at the intersection of two taxiways.

Sources: FAA (link above); ABC News (link above)

4. WIDER CONTEXT: HOW THIS KIND OF COLLISION HAPPENS

Aviation safety literature describes taxiway and runway confusion as arising when crews act on the clearance they expect rather than the one actually received, fail to cross-check and copy taxi and hold-short instructions, or face workload and distraction at hot spots. Uncertainty over taxi routes or low-visibility procedures adds further risk.

The recommended defences in that literature include verbalising and recording clearances, cross-checking instructions, and requesting progressive taxi when in doubt.

Sources: Flight Safety Foundation, "Erasing Confusion" (https://t.co/1Co6hbtg1T); Eurocontrol / Flight Safety Foundation Global Action Plan for the Prevention of Runway Incursions (https://t.co/bOK1wAlnT4); U.S. GAO via https://t.co/ivLfzsiCI7 (https://t.co/azL60tHbDi)

🦦On November 16, 2026, as U.S. airlines worked to restore normal operations after days of disruption, United Airlines reported a widespread system outage that grounded departures and left passengers stranded on tarmacs.

The airline confirmed the issue in an official statement on X, apologizing for the inconvenience and noting that teams were working to restore systems. Passengers were advised to monitor flight status through the United app or https://t.co/YR3asExCao. Reports from travelers described aircraft unable to obtain critical takeoff performance and weight-and-balance data, forcing planes to return to gates or remain on the runway.

This latest setback arrived just as the broader aviation system was recovering from a rare nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration on the afternoon of November 13. That stoppage, lasting roughly four and a half to five hours, marked the longest nationwide halt to U.S. air travel since the September 11, 2001 attacks. It was triggered when a contractor upgrade of aging copper wiring to fiber-optic cable at a remote FAA facility near El Dorado, Arkansas, caused a router to flood the network with approximately 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. The cascade affected systems linked to a recently replaced router in Amarillo, Texas, creating instability at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers and prompting the FAA to halt departures nationwide as a precaution.

Officials, including Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, stated there was no evidence of a cyberattack. The FAA lifted the ground stop around 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday, but the effects lingered through the weekend. FlightAware data showed more than 12,000 cancellations on Friday alone, with totals exceeding 17,000 cancellations by Sunday in what ranked as one of the worst technology-related airline disruptions in decades, surpassing the scale of Southwest Airlines’ 2022 systems meltdown. JetBlue and American Airlines were among the hardest hit by percentage and volume, while United, Delta, and Southwest experienced lower but still significant cancellation rates of roughly 3 to 5 percent on Sunday amid thousands of additional delays.

By Monday morning, cancellations and delays had declined substantially as airlines repositioned aircraft and crews. Duffy and other officials had projected a return closer to normal by the start of the week. The separate United outage, however, underscored the fragility of both national air traffic control infrastructure and individual airline systems after years of deferred modernization. United CEO Scott Kirby had earlier called for greater investment in air traffic control technology, noting bipartisan interest in addressing longstanding gaps in redundancy and reliability.

For travelers, the practical guidance remains consistent: check status directly with the airline, expect possible delays or rebookings, and monitor official channels for updates as restoration efforts continue. The episode highlights how interconnected technical vulnerabilities, whether in shared air traffic networks or carrier-specific operations, can rapidly compound into widespread passenger disruption.

Yesterday X started paying people to clip other people's videos. Agencies charge online stores $400 and up for one 30-second AI ad. One clip that took 20 minutes to edit paid $10,300. An AI render of that kind of video costs about 30 cents.
Apps, skincare lines and software companies buy these videos every day, and you no longer need a camera or a crew to make them. In one @Picsart account you can paste a product link and get a talking AI creator, a script, lip-sync and captions, then sell that ad to a store. Pro costs $10.50 a month billed yearly: https://picsart.go.link/faNX7 
I read every payout thread, creator contract and case study I could find on X, about 60 of them, including the ones from this week. This guide turns them into four paths you can start now, with the scripts, prompts and rates to copy. Bookmark it. You'll want it open the day you pick your path.
 
Why brands pay for this
A normal paid ad costs a brand $20 to $30 for every 1,000 people it reaches. Creator campaigns run at $0.16 to $1 per 1,000 views. One app got 830 million views in about four months on a total spend of $250,000.
Demand is climbing. On Fiverr, searches for AI UGC video ads grew 265% in six months. A human UGC video costs $150 to $300, and agencies charge $400 to $900 for one AI ad. Yesterday Greg Isenberg showed AI agents making UGC videos for $4 that used to cost $500:
 
The platforms pay far less. Fruit Love Island's team says TikTok paid about $15 per million views. Another creator got $626 from TikTok for 42 million views, because only 5% of them came from regions that pay.
 
Creators on X compare what 1 million views pays, and the estimates swing a lot: $0 to $1,500 from the platforms, around $3,000 from brand-paid clipping campaigns. This post with the numbers got 3 million views on its own:
 
So three of the four paths below end with a brand paying you. The fourth pays you for your audience.
Pick your path first
 
Good at writing and don't want to show your face: AI UGC for brands
Willing to wait 2 months for a bigger upside: your own AI character
Comfortable on camera with a phone: canvas UGC
No money, no product, want the first payment fast: clipping, now built into X
Pick one. People who post their results almost all ran one path for a full month before adding a second.
Path 1: AI UGC for brands
Same videos, no camera. You render a realistic AI person talking about a product and sell the video to the store. No followers, no monetized channel, and your country doesn't have to be on TikTok's payout list.
 
In Picsart the price of a render depends on the model and the resolution. Pro works out to about 2 cents a credit. 10 seconds on MiniMax H3 Max Turbo at 480p is about 10 credits, and 5 seconds of Seedance 2.5 at 480p is 20. That puts a hook at about 30 cents. The same 5 seconds of Seedance cost 90 credits at 1080p, so draft at 480p and pay for 1080p only once the shot works.
Budget for rejects. The director of Kalshi's NBA Finals ad, reported at about $2,000, needed 300 to 400 generations for 15 usable clips.
One creator's version of a 30-cent ad, with the full workflow in the post:
 
Step 1: Write the script before you render anything
Brands pay for the script. One creator's first five AI videos got 300 views each. After a rewrite with this prompt, the same format hit 40,000:
 
Most of the work is the first sentence. An app founder who ran 60 creators watched the same person go from a few hundred views to hundreds of thousands by changing only that line. Write five hooks of five types: a problem said out loud, a surprising result, "I didn't believe it until", a comparison with what they use now, and an objection answered head-on.
Step 2: Make the ad in Picsart UGC Ads
Paste the product link or upload a photo, pick an avatar and a format: talking head, review, unboxing, testimonial, street interview or app demo. It writes a script you can replace with yours, then adds lip-synced dialogue, product shots and captions.
Picsart's own demos show the flow: product and settings on one side, the finished ad on the other.
 
Viewers decide it's AI in the first second, usually for one of four reasons: a face they've seen 40 times this week, a studio voice coming out of a kitchen, a person who never blinks or moves their hands, or a setting that doesn't fit the claim. Put skincare in a bathroom, supplements in a kitchen and software at a desk. A car is the easiest scene to render, because it's small and evenly lit, and nothing moves behind the person.
Then check every second by eye: the hands, the shape of the product, any text on the label. AI still garbles small text, and the client will see it first. Run your versions past Vera, Picsart's ad-testing agent built with the research firm Zappi, and fix the weakest in the first 3 seconds. Resize Pro makes 9:16, 4:5 and 1:1.
Step 3: Use one face for one brand
A face that drifts between videos kills the account, because nobody recognizes the person. In Picsart, the Character creator in Storyspace builds a 4-view sheet (front, side, back and a close-up) and saves the character, so new renders start from the same reference. Faces can still drift, so watch each take. Match the face to the claim, too: a 22-year-old talking about joint pain loses the viewer before the script starts.
If you'd rather write the character yourself, start here:
 
One action per shot. If she walks, laughs, turns and waves in the same prompt, the model mixes them up.
Step 4: Find stores that already buy ads
Open the Meta Ad Library, which is free and needs no login. Search a niche word like "skincare" or "dog treats", set the status to active and look for stores with many image ads and little video. They test a lot and are short on video to test. Save 30 to 50 before you write to anyone. Then put up a Fiverr gig: AI UGC video ads for your store, 3 hooks, 48 hours.
Step 5: Send the ad first and sell a pack
Make one free 15-second ad for the best store, label it as AI, and send it with your rate:
 
$400 for 5 ads is $80 an ad, inside the $75 to $150 that published rate cards list. A monthly plan of 12 ads goes for $1,200. One creator's example: 2 packs in month one come to about $775 after the plan, and 2 packs plus 3 monthly clients in month three come to about $4,375. A friend of that creator closed two perfume videos for $400.
This is what a single AI product video can do with no ad spend behind it:
 
Path 2: Your own AI character
The slowest path and the one with the most upside, because the audience belongs to you. One of the most-read articles on this topic this year, over 18 million views, sets a target of $10,000 in two to three months. Another author built an AI influencer for $0 and started monetizing in the first week.
This is the kind of video they're built on: a girl who doesn't exist, 2 million views.
 
The characters that travel have one look you can recognize from a single frame. A man with a rose on a mall escalator: 12.8 million plays on an account with 48,000 followers and 13 posts. A giant in glasses and white trousers: 35.7 million. A man in a pink glitter suit with a tiny dog: 9.5 million.
Step 1: Design the character
You can start for $0. Picsart TV gives a free account free generations every day, and SANA-Sprint images cost 0 credits. In Storyspace, pick a human, an alien, a monster or an animal, then shape the face, hair, outfit and accessories. Lock what you like and shuffle the rest. Save the sheet. Each prompt from then on only describes what changes.
Write one line that changes every episode. If you can't, you have one clip and no character.
Step 2: Make the first 20 videos
Use four beats: an ordinary setup, one small accident, a reaction from whoever feels it most, then a twist. A 10-second clip where a man swats a mosquito and her groom in a top hat cries over the body needs no words.
Take a clip of your own with good movement and use Recast to swap in your character. Or render the first frame and animate it with one action in AI Playground, where Kling 3.0, Seedance 2.5 and the other big models share one credit balance:
 
If a scene fails after 3 to 5 tries, change the scene instead of repeating the prompt. A perfect talking head isn't required either: clay, cartoon and story formats regularly beat realistic ones, because people stop for the idea.
Step 3: Post daily and chase one 100,000-view video
Post every day on TikTok, Reels and X. The first videos get 300 to 500 views, and that is normal. Once one video passes 100,000, stop testing new ideas and make variations of that one.
TikTok's payout program ignores videos under a minute, so one author has Marc, Picsart's montage agent, cut six clips into a 70-second countdown, and turns each week into a 10-minute YouTube episode. Their model for a month: $11,196 at 300,000 to 400,000 views an upload, about $1,450 at 50,000.
Step 4: Get paid without finding a brand first
Earn with Picsart pays for original posts you make with Picsart tools on your own Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and X. There is no follower minimum, you see the payout formula before you start, and it has paid over $1 million to 80,000+ creators, with the top ones at up to $10,000 a month. It's open in North America, Southeast Asia and Brazil. Each campaign has its own brief, so check what it allows.
Picsart also runs challenges: $150,000 in prize pools in September and October alone, including $10,000 for each of five microdrama winners. Put "AI creator" in the bio from day one.
Halfway through. If you know someone who keeps saying they should do something with AI video, send them this.
Path 3: Canvas UGC with your phone
"Canvas" means a blank account. You open a fresh TikTok or Instagram account for one brand, post one format 1 to 3 times a day and get paid per video. The feed barely looks at follower count, so a new account can reach strangers in its first week.

Path 4: Clipping, now built into X
Clippers cut long videos (podcasts, streams, founders talking) into short clips and post them on their own pages. Since yesterday you can do it inside X, in the iOS and Android apps. It's still rolling out, so update the app if you don't see it yet. Tap Repost, then Clip video, pick 5 to 60 seconds from any video longer than 2 minutes, add your take and post. The clip credits the original and links back, and both you and the creator earn from its views through Original Content Rewards.
 
X hasn't said what a clip pays yet. The rates you can count on today come from campaign platforms, where brands and creators pay $0.16 to $1 per 1,000 views, some up to $5, with a cap of $300 to $600 per clip. Take campaigns that pay at least $0.50 per 1,000 views with a cap of $300 or more.
On X, start with the biggest business, tech and AI podcasts that post full episodes there. Clip the hot take, the number nobody expected or the argument, 20 to 60 seconds, with 1 to 3 lines of your own on top. Once your clips pull views, offer the podcast a monthly fee to clip every episode.
For TikTok, Reels and Shorts, Picsart's AI Video Clipping turns a video of 10 minutes or longer into up to 12 short clips with captions, and pricing goes by the upload rather than by clip. Picsart Earn lists clipping campaigns too.
Every clip has to pass the stranger test: it has to work for someone who has never seen the stream.
 
Post 3 to 5 a day, submit every link, judge a clip on day three, and after 2 weeks keep the 2 clip types with the most views. Only 13 of 80 clippers on one campaign posted on more than one platform, so that alone puts you ahead. The clipper who ranked first out of 80,000 on one platform last year says one of their students got paid $10,300 for a single clip that took 20 minutes to edit.
Three people, three paths, their real months
 
The clipper: posted 1,000 clips in one month across 12 pages before ranking first of 80,000. A student's best single clip paid $10,300.
The AI character: 5 days to the first paying subscriber, then one reel at 600,000 views. $600 in month one, $5,300 in month two, about 40 minutes of work a day.
The Shorts channel: 330.3 million views and $33,803 in estimated revenue in under 90 days, on about $300 of AI video.

A chat model for scripts and prompts: $20 a month
A phone you already have, plus a second cheap one if you film canvas UGC: $0 to $100

Charge by the video until you have one video over 500,000 views. After that, ask for a monthly floor plus a share of results. When a brand wants to run your video as a paid ad, that is a separate permission, so ask for 30 to 50% on top before you sign.
Your first 30 days
Week 1: Pick one path. Save 20 videos in your niche that beat their account's average views, and write down the hook and the first 3 seconds of each
Week 2: Post or render one video a day in the format that showed up most. Don't judge anything before video 20.
Week 3: Take the video that did best and make five versions of it, changing one thing at a time: the hook, the setting, the length.
Week 4: Send that video to 30 brands a day with your rate. About 1 in 100 cold messages gets a reply, so 30 a day gets you about two conversations a week.
Questions people always ask
Do I need followers? No. None of the four paths needs an audience to start, and Earn has no follower minimum.
Can I post AI UGC without saying it's AI? Don't. Say "AI creator" in the bio, tell the brand, and mark paid posts as ads where the platform asks.
How long until the first dollar? From the published numbers: 1 to 3 weeks for clipping, 2 to 4 weeks for canvas and AI UGC, 1 to 2 months for your own character. Many people earn nothing in that time, so treat these as the good cases.
Where people lose money
Views without buyers. One founder saw 0.5% of downloads from UGC turn into paying users, against 7% from ads. Creators who can show downloads or sales get renewed.
Mass-produced repeats. YouTube's inauthentic content rule cuts monetization from videos that look the same every time. One author throws away a quarter to a third of each batch for that reason.
Quitting at video 7. One creator nearly quit after 7 videos and found the format by video 20.
Pick the path that matches what you already have, copy a format that already has 20 winners in your niche, and post 20 videos before you change anything.

Your AI 3D demo isn’t done until Godot can play it.
Not “generate a mesh.”
 Not “export a file and pray.”
 A real clear: the .glb is in the Godot project, the node is instanced, collision exists if gameplay needs it, and Play doesn’t scream.
Claude Code can speedrun that whole loop — Blender → GLB → running scene — in about ninety minutes, if you route it like a category run instead of an art demo.
Unity teams fight a DCC→editor seam with import settings and prefab religion. Godot teams fight a different boss: files on disk are almost the whole API. Drop a GLB in the right folder, let the importer breathe, instance it, run. That makes Godot weirdly perfect for agent speedruns — if you route the run correctly.
This piece is a 90-minute route, not a stack essay. Three myths to skip, five acts on the clock, one prompt that encodes the clear condition.
 
Myth board (cross these out before you start)
Myth 1: “If it looks good in Blender, Godot will be fine.”
 Godot will import something. Fine is meters, +Y up, applied modifiers, clean names, and a human who opened the running game.
Myth 2: “FBX is the grown-up format.”
 For Godot 4, GLB is the default adult. One blob. Materials packed. Fewer texture scavenger hunts. Keep FBX for the rare pipeline that demands it  not for superstition.
Myth 3: “The agent should author the whole game in the Godot editor UI.”
 Optional. Many strong setups write GDScript and scenes as files, use Godot MCP mainly to run and read debug output, and use Blender MCP for the mesh/material last mile. Screenshots are nice. print() and error logs are underrated eyes.
 
Cross the myths. Now the clock.
Act 0 — Boot (0:00–0:12)
Goal: tools answer, not art.
You want Claude Code talking to:
Blender via MCP (mcp-for-blender / BlenderMCP addon started in the N-panel)
Godot via run/debug MCP (e.g. @coding-solo/godot-mcp), or Play manually while Claude owns files + Blender
 
Boot checks, in order:
Blender: scene_info returns objects. Screenshot/look works.
Godot path: project opens; a trivial run prints something you recognize.
Folder contract exists: e.g. assets/models/ for GLBs, art/CREDITS.md for licenses.
Save the .blend. Save the Godot project.
If boot fails, do not “just try a dragon.” Fix the socket.
Act I — Brief like a split (0:12–0:20)
Minimum brief fields: gameplay job, meters, tri budget, style, origin, export path inside Godot repo, collision yes/no, clear condition.
Claude must echo the brief back before modeling.
Act II — Blender segment (0:20–0:55)
Inspect → blockout → refine → materials → look → prep → export selection as GLB (+Y up) into assets/models/ inside the Godot project.
Stop when file is on disk, tris/bounds reported, look inspected.
 
Act III — Godot segment (0:55–1:15)
Confirm .glb in FileSystem
Instance into scene
Add collision if needed
Run, read debug, fix
Report paths, tris, credits
 
Act IV — Clear screen (1:15–1:30)
CLEAR means: meters OK, GLB path real, collision if needed, quiet run, credits if needed, human glanced once.
 
The category-winning prompt
 

Your AI 3D demo isn’t done until Godot can play it.

The only prestige category is CLEAR  not the bevel.
